facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Stream deposits are a non-debt claim that creditors should track. facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Operating execution is the near-term swing factor and is currently mixed. In the second quarter port closures deferred concentrate shipments in Peru to July, a hoist gearbox failure and reduced workforce availability held back Manitoba, and Copper Mountain ran with its primary SAG mill constrained, with a cash cost of USD 3.22 per pound against an annual guidance range of USD 1.50 to USD 2.50. Adjusted EBITDA fell from USD 421.9 million in the first quarter to USD 321.2 million in the second, so execution rather than ownership is what moves creditor risk this year. Basis: 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 2, 5, 10–14; calculation BG-05

facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence against the supportive view is that capital allocation, not ownership, now carries the risk. Hudbay has two development projects in Arizona, an expansion in British Columbia and a Nevada project, the Copper World study is expected to show higher capital cost than the 2023 pre-feasibility study, and there is no sponsor to inject equity if a project overruns. facts.label: Transaction summary and new debt issues
facts.text: Copper World joint venture. Hudbay sold a 30% interest in Copper World to Mitsubishi in January 2026 under a subscription agreement dated 12 August 2025, for USD 600 million in total, of which USD 422.7 million of cash was received at closing and a further USD 180 million is due within 18 months. The transaction was accounted for as an equity transaction, so Hudbay keeps control and consolidates the project, and the cash received is reserved for the project and not available for general group use. facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Earnings are volatile and concentrated in two operations, which is the risk a creditor underwrites, not leverage. Adjusted EBITDA has ranged by a factor of 2.96x between the weakest and strongest of 11 quarters, and Peru and Manitoba earned 85.1% of first-half 2026 revenue. In the third quarter of 2025 mandatory wildfire evacuations shut Manitoba for most of the quarter, a temporary mill suspension hit Peru and a USD 60 million concentrate shipment slipped into the next quarter, taking revenue down 35.3% and adjusted EBITDA to USD 142.6 million. In the second quarter of 2026 port closures again deferred a concentrate shipment to July, and a 19.5% fall in copper sold cut adjusted EBITDA 23.9%. Even so, debt would be 0.92x the trailing EBITDA at the end of the third quarter of 2025, the lowest of the last five quarter-ends, 1.05x the 2024 level and 1.51x if four quarters matched the weakest, so interruptions threaten liquidity timing before they threaten solvency. facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Gold by-product credits, not copper, are what make Hudbay a low-cost producer, which ties creditor risk to the gold price. In the second quarter of 2026 gold credits were 78.3% of all by-product credits and paid for 85.1% of the gross cash cost of USD 4.57 per pound, so the reported net cost of negative USD 0.40 per pound would be USD 3.50 without them; in the first quarter of 2026, with more gold sold, it was negative USD 1.80. Gross cash cost per pound rose 22.8% in a year on fuel and consumables, and the 2026 cost guidance assumes gold at USD 3,850 per ounce, so the cost position is a bet on gold holding at or above that level. Gold was 38% of 2025 revenue. facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Production is stable at group level but its mix is moving away from the gold-rich Pampacancha ore, and guidance needs a stronger second half. Pampacancha was fully mined by December 2025, so Peru gold guidance is 76.5% below 2025 and Peru copper 3.1% below, while the group midpoint is 4.9% higher for copper and 8.7% lower for gold. First-half output is 45.3% of the copper midpoint and 46.2% of the gold midpoint, and the second-half plan depends on British Columbia reaching its target throughput once the primary grinding mill returns, on higher Manitoba grades and on the Peru pebble crushers. Management states that it has met copper guidance for 11 consecutive years, which supports the plan but does not test a second half this heavily loaded. facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Cash conversion is moderate because taxes and capital absorb most of EBITDA. Taxes paid in the first half of 2026 were USD 262.8 million, 35.4% of adjusted EBITDA against 30.3% a year earlier, with tax expense at 43.1% of income before tax, so operating cash flow before working capital was 56.4% of adjusted EBITDA against 67.1%. Company-defined free cash flow of USD 413.0 million over the last 12 months is 32.5% of adjusted EBITDA, and the first-half working-capital inflow of USD 89.5 million is probably partly timing, because the concentrate deferred from the second quarter was delivered in July. Higher profits therefore bring higher tax outflows, and deleveraging capacity after growth spending is smaller than EBITDA suggests. facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence against the supportive view is that leverage is measured on trailing adjusted EBITDA that the company calls a record, struck at high metal prices, while the cost advantage and the profit after tax both depend on gold. If gold fell below the USD 3,850 per ounce assumed in 2026 guidance while a Peru or Manitoba interruption recurred, quarterly EBITDA could return towards the USD 142.6 million seen in 2025 just as USD 600.0 million of group-funded capital, Copper World and the 2028 and 2029 maturities converge. The view would weaken if the sanction decision commits group cash beyond the USD 200 million estimate, if the revolver is drawn again to fund growth, or if covenant levels prove tight on a definition the company does not print. It would strengthen if the USD 272.0 million draw were repaid from cash flow, if the 2028 and 2029 maturities were refinanced early, and if covenant levels showed wide headroom. facts.label: Business model, ownership and revenue durability
facts.text: Revenue is durable in volume but not in price: Hudbay sells copper, gold, silver, zinc and molybdenum priced off market quotations, and receivables on provisionally priced concentrate are marked to forward prices each quarter, so revenue moves with metal markets rather than contracts. Copper and gold together were 90.6% of revenue from contracts in the first half, Peru and Manitoba earned 85.1% of revenue, and 38% of 2025 revenue was gold. The sources do not name customers, state offtake terms or show a customer concentration, so buyer concentration is not established. The consequence for creditors is high operating leverage to prices with low contractual visibility, offset by 90.8% terminable commitments and low leverage. facts.label: Cost structure and margin resilience
facts.text: Margins can be defended against moderate volume shortfalls, since adjusted EBITDA margin was 50.9% in the second quarter of 2026 against 55.7% in the first after revenue fell 16.6%, and they are exposed to input inflation and to gold. Onsite cost per pound rose 25.9% in a year to USD 4.23, on higher fuel and consumable prices and, in British Columbia, equipment maintenance timing, and the second quarter showed operating deleverage as adjusted EBITDA fell 23.9% on a 19.5% fall in copper sold. Three features cushion the margin: employee profit sharing, which reached USD 36.1 million in the fourth quarter of 2025 at high margins and was lower in Peru in the second quarter of 2026; a new Peru power contract and lower treatment and refining charges; and a record British Columbia mining rate. Adjusted EBITDA margin has ranged from 41.1% to 55.7% across the periods supplied. Basis: 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 2, 9, 13, 26; 6-K-EX-99.3_2025-12-31_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 4, 34; calculation FC-06; calculation FC-07; calculation FC-08

facts.label: Market forces and policy
facts.text: Five forces matter to credit mainly through price-taking, entry barriers and input costs. Rivalry and substitutes act through metal prices, which Hudbay does not set, and its hedges are small. New entrants face long permitting, as the New Ingerbelle permit and the judicial review application against it show, which protects the existing production base but delays Hudbay's own growth. Buyer power cannot be assessed because customers are not named, and substitutes are not discussed in the sources. Supplier power shows in fuel and consumable inflation, Manitoba labour shortages that required a mining contractor, and equipment failures such as a hoist gearbox, each of which raised unit costs in the second quarter of 2026. Basis: 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 9, 11–12, 19–20; 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-03-31_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 14–15; 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-06-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, page 28; calculation FC-06; calculation FC-15

facts.label: Outlook
facts.text: The outlook for the next 12 months to 24 months is supportive but back-end loaded. Tailwinds are the delivery of concentrate deferred into July, the second-half ramp-up in British Columbia, higher Manitoba output, the Peru pebble crushers, copper hedges struck above the copper price assumed in guidance, improved consolidated cost guidance of negative USD 0.45 to negative USD 0.25 per pound, and the higher Constancia mill permit. Headwinds are fuel and consumable costs, dependence on a repaired primary grinding mill in British Columbia, Manitoba labour, cash taxes and the higher capital plan. These support liquidity and margins in the near term and leave the second-half guidance exposed to execution. facts.text: The outlook for three to five years turns on timing. facts.label: Downside scenario
facts.text: The realistic downside is a repeat of the 2025 sequence while gold weakens and Copper World spending begins. The initiating condition is a fall in gold below the USD 3,850 per ounce used for 2026 guidance together with an interruption in Peru or Manitoba, both of which occurred within 12 months. The first operational break is deferred shipments or a mine shutdown, as in the third quarter of 2025, when revenue fell 35.3% and adjusted EBITDA fell to USD 142.6 million. Lower gold credits then raise net cash cost directly, since every dollar of gold credit lost falls straight to EBITDA, while the cash tax charge falls only with profit. Free cash flow turns negative for a quarter, as it did in the third quarter of 2025, and the revolver, with USD 153.7 million undrawn, absorbs the gap. Leverage would be 0.92x on the trailing EBITDA at the weakest recent quarter-end, 1.05x on the 2024 level and 1.51x on four weak quarters. Management can cancel USD 183.9 million of commitments, defer Cactus and Mason spending and keep dividends at their small level, so resilience looks sufficient to avoid liquidity distress through 2027 on the stated figures. The observable triggers are quarterly EBITDA below USD 142.6 million, further revolver draws, a Copper World sanction without committed non-group funding, and no refinancing plan by late 2027. facts.label: Overall credit view
facts.text: Overall, Hudbay presents an adequate business profile supported by low leverage, a gold-driven cost position and cancellable capital commitments, but credit quality is constrained by concentration in two operations, exposure to gold and copper prices and a growth programme that peaks as its debt matures. Cash-flow durability appears adequate because company-defined free cash flow of USD 413.0 million over the last 12 months has absorbed taxes and sustaining capital, but conversion falls as profits rise. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on metal prices in 2027, the Copper World outcome and covenant headroom that the sources do not show. The primary downside path is a gold price fall or a Peru or Manitoba interruption coinciding with Copper World funding and the 2028 and 2029 maturities. Further analysis would require covenant levels, the audited 2025 statements, the Copper World venture and Wheaton agreements, customer terms and market evidence on pricing and ratings. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation FC-01; calculation FC-09; calculation FC-12

facts.label: Strengths and weaknesses
facts.text: Strengths, in order of weight. First, low leverage with no principal due before 2028: debt of USD 860.2 million is 0.68x adjusted EBITDA, so a weak year would not by itself threaten debt service. Second, a gold-driven cost position: credits paid for 85.1% of gross cash cost, which kept adjusted EBITDA at 50.9% to 55.7% of revenue in 2026, though it depends on gold. Third, liquidity and flexibility: USD 710.1 million of liquidity excluding Copper World cash and 90.8% of capital commitments that can be cancelled give management levers in a downturn. Fourth, creditor-aligned financial policy: debt fell USD 148.4 million in the first half, the dividend is 1.1% of operating cash flow and no sponsor is identified, which lowers the risk of cash extraction. facts.text: Weaknesses, in order of weight. First, concentration and interruption record: 85.1% of revenue comes from Peru and Manitoba and adjusted EBITDA has ranged by a factor of 2.96x between quarters, so cash flow can fall fast. Fourth, cash leakage: taxes paid were 35.4% of first-half adjusted EBITDA. Fifth, opacity: no covenant levels, guarantor structure or ranking of USD 324.5 million of other claims. facts.label: Strengths and weaknesses
facts.text: The nine-dimension profile is as follows. Scale and market position is average: revenue was USD 2,211.0 million in 2025 across three regions, but Hudbay sets no prices. Competitive advantage is average: the cost position rests on by-product credits, not on a structural moat. Business diversification is average: five metals and three regions, but 85.1% of revenue from two operations. Cost and capex flexibility is average: 90.8% of commitments can be terminated, but gross cost per pound rose 22.8%. Margin stability is average: adjusted EBITDA margin ranged from 41.1% to 55.7%. Free cash flow stability is average: the quarter-to-quarter swing is wide and conversion is 32.5% of EBITDA. Ability to refinance is average: a USD 52.0 million municipal bond was placed in June 2026 at 4.5%, but no rating or market quote was supplied. Liquidity is strong on the company's definition: USD 1,044.6 million, or 0.83x total debt after removing reserved cash, and no maturity before 2028. Financial policy and governance is average: creditor-friendly behaviour with unseen covenants and restricted-payment limits. The trend is improving leverage and thinner revolver availability, and the key missing data are covenants, audited 2025 statements, customer terms and market evidence. ## Findings
### Bottom line

The seven supplied Hudbay filings are enough for a consolidated credit snapshot to 30 June 2026, but not for covenant, ranking or guarantor-level work, so creditors should read every leverage and liquidity figure as a consolidated, company-defined measure.
Basis: 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-06-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, pages 1, 18–19; 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 6–7

## Findings
### Bottom line

Hudbay is lightly levered, with total debt at 0.56x reported last-twelve-month EBITDA on 30 June 2026, but USD 334.5 million of its cash is reserved for Copper World, so creditors should anchor on net debt excluding that cash, at 0.24x adjusted EBITDA.

### Key findings

Leverage is low on every definition the sources support, and it fell in the first half of 2026 as the 2026 notes were repaid and trailing earnings rose. Total debt to reported last-twelve-month EBITDA moved from 0.74x at the end of 2025 to 0.56x at 30 June 2026, and total debt to the company's adjusted EBITDA moved from 0.95x to 0.68x, as total debt fell by USD 148.4 million and adjusted last-twelve-month EBITDA rose from USD 1,060.9 million to USD 1,271.6 million. Reported EBITDA of USD 1,541.4 million is the higher figure because the USD 322.3 million impairment reversal on Copper World booked in the third quarter of 2025 is still in the trailing year; the adjusted figure removes it, so the adjusted ratio is the better guide to repeatable leverage.

Basis: 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-06-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, page 18; 6-K-EX-99.3_2025-12-31_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 10, 40; 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 24–25; calculation C-03; calculation C-04; calculation C-06; calculation C-08; calculation C-19

The headline net cash position rests on money the wider group cannot use. Cash of USD 890.9 million at 30 June 2026 includes USD 334.5 million held by Copper World LLC for the project's exclusive use, and the company also deducts USD 49.8 million of restricted municipal bond proceeds to report net debt of negative USD 80.5 million. Counting only cash available to the wider group, net debt is USD 303.8 million, or 0.24x adjusted EBITDA, against the company's negative 0.1x. The revolver is secured on substantially all assets other than those of the Copper World, Mason and Cactus projects and the notes are not guaranteed by the subsidiaries holding those projects, so Copper World's cash does not support those lenders directly, while the USD 50.7 million of Copper World municipal bonds, guaranteed by the parent, sits inside total debt.
Basis: 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-06-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, pages 12, 14, 18–20; 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 7, 24–25; calculation C-05; calculation C-11

The debt stack is short and simple, with no principal due before 2028. It comprises USD 272.0 million drawn under secured revolving facilities that mature in November 2028 and carry a USD 450.0 million commitment, USD 542.4 million of senior notes due in April 2029 and USD 52.0 million of municipal bonds whose initial mandatory tender date is in 2036. The April 2026 repayment of the USD 472.5 million 2026 notes used cash and the revolver draw, so USD 270.1 million of secured bank debt now ranks ahead of the unsecured notes, and cumulative debt through the notes is 0.53x reported EBITDA. The revolver and the notes mature within five months of each other, so the refinancing window opens in 2028. Principal exceeds carrying value by USD 6.2 million of unamortised issuance costs and discounts.
Basis: 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-06-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, pages 18–20; 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-03-31_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, page 13; calculation C-09; calculation C-15

Liquidity is adequate on the company's definition and thinner on the group's usable basis. Cash of USD 890.9 million and USD 153.7 million of undrawn revolver availability give USD 1,044.6 million, or 1.21x total debt; without Copper World's reserved cash the figure is USD 710.1 million, or 0.83x total debt. Undrawn availability fell from USD 425.2 million at 31 March 2026 to USD 153.7 million because of the USD 272.0 million draw. Outstanding capital commitments of USD 202.6 million are mostly terminable, so most near-term capital calls can be cancelled, and the sources print no covenant levels against which headroom could be measured.

Basis: 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-06-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, pages 19, 29; 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-03-31_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, page 14; 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 1, 3, 6; calculation C-10; calculation C-11; calculation C-17

Interest cover is very high but rests on half-year evidence. Calculated reported EBITDA of USD 713.6 million covered cash interest paid of USD 30.0 million 23.79x in the first half of 2026, against 18.17x in the first half of 2025, as EBITDA rose 31.3% and cash interest was almost unchanged. The first-quarter cash flow statements print no interest line, which suggests interest is paid in lumps outside that quarter, so quarterly and last-twelve-month cover cannot be worked, and no full-year 2025 cash interest figure is supplied. Interest on the repaid 2026 notes drops out of later periods, partly offset by interest on the revolver draw, whose margin the sources do not print.
Basis: 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-06-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, pages 2–3; 6-K-EX-99.1_2025-09-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, page 43; calculation C-07; calculation C-14

Cash conversion is moderate and was helped by working capital in the second quarter. Net cash from operating activities was USD 508.3 million in the first half of 2026, including a USD 89.5 million working-capital inflow, after USD 262.8 million of cash taxes. Purchases of property, plant and equipment of USD 293.1 million left free cash flow, defined here as operating cash flow less those purchases, of USD 215.2 million, or 30.2% of reported EBITDA. The second-quarter working-capital inflow of USD 86.9 million partly reflects trade receivables falling to USD 163.1 million as concentrate shipments from Peru were delayed by port closures and delivered in July, so part of it is likely to reverse.
Basis: 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-06-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, pages 2–3, 12–13; 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, page 5; calculation C-13

Total debt understates the claims on cash flow. Outside the USD 860.2 million total, the company carries lease liabilities of USD 53.0 million, equipment and land financing of USD 131.3 million that rose from USD 92.2 million at the end of 2025, deferred land payments of USD 102.8 million assumed with Arizona Sonoran, deferred and contingent Copper Mountain consideration of USD 29.1 million and a USD 8.3 million Wheaton refund liability, together USD 324.5 million. The land payments are secured vendor carryback loans at 6% with USD 82.2 million due on 28 August 2029, so with all of these items total debt would be USD 1,184.7 million, or 0.93x adjusted EBITDA, and the land loans are secured by deeds of trust on Cactus land. Decommissioning, restoration and similar liabilities of USD 336.7 million and pension and other employee benefit obligations of USD 86.1 million are further long-dated claims outside debt.
Basis: 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-06-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, pages 15–17; calculation C-12

Stream deposits are a non-debt claim that creditors should track. Deferred revenue was USD 297.1 million at 30 June 2026, down from USD 317.1 million at the end of 2025, and is settled in precious metals rather than cash, but the company accretes USD 9.0 million of finance cost on it in the half year and carries a USD 8.3 million Wheaton refund liability on the stream for a mine that has finished mining, repayable in cash by 2052 if metal credits fall short. Amortising USD 29.0 million of the balance into revenue lifts reported EBITDA, and the adjusted measure deducts it.
Basis: 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-06-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, pages 1–2, 15, 17, 20–21; calculation C-12

Two transactions reshaped the balance sheet in 2026, mostly through equity and cash rather than debt. The Copper World joint venture closed in January 2026 with USD 422.7 million of cash received at closing and USD 169.8 million of deferred consideration recorded as a receivable, and Mitsubishi's 30% interest is a non-controlling interest of USD 463.4 million. The Arizona Sonoran acquisition on 24 June 2026 added USD 1,357.0 million of exploration property for new shares valued at USD 1,135.6 million plus shares already held, and brought USD 102.8 million of deferred land payments. The only later event is a dividend of C$0.01 per share declared on 28 July 2026, which cannot be converted to US dollars from the sources.
Basis: 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-06-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, pages 8–9; 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, page 22; calculation C-16

Four data conflicts affect how the figures can be used, though none changes the leverage conclusion. The fourth-quarter 2025 release called USD 1,008.6 million total principal debt, but that is the carrying value, and note principal was USD 1,014.9 million. Free cash flow comparatives differ between releases, for example USD 228.2 million against USD 225.0 million for the fourth quarter of 2025. Fourth-quarter 2025 cash from operations is USD 209.4 million in one release and USD 290.4 million in a trailing table whose own total implies USD 209.4 million. First-quarter 2026 adjusted net earnings are USD 159.1 million in one release and USD 161.0 million in the next. Trailing cash-flow measures should therefore be read with a margin of a few USD million.

Basis: 6-K-EX-99.3_2025-12-31_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 22, 41; 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 24–25; 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-03-31_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, page 24; Source readiness (CP-0)
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest contrary evidence is that reported leverage ignores Copper World. The project's cash of USD 334.5 million is spoken for, the sanction decision is expected in late 2026, and the group's own net debt of USD 303.8 million will rise with any group funding of the project, so 0.24x adjusted EBITDA is a starting point rather than a ceiling. The view would weaken if the sanction decision commits the group to fund Copper World from the revolver, whose availability is already USD 153.7 million, and it would strengthen if the USD 272.0 million draw were repaid from operating cash flow.
Basis: 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-06-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, pages 12, 29; 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 1, 3–4; calculation C-10; calculation C-11

Earnings are also cyclical: adjusted EBITDA fell from USD 421.9 million in the first quarter of 2026 to USD 321.2 million in the second on lower sales volumes, and results lean on high gold and copper prices. A sustained fall in prices or a repeat of operating interruptions would cut EBITDA, and total debt to adjusted EBITDA, now 0.68x, would rise. The audited 2025 statements, the revolver covenant levels and the Copper World feasibility study are the documents that would most change the view.
Basis: 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 3, 5, 24; calculation C-18

- The audited 2025 financial statements are not supplied, so for the FY2025 column mine operating costs, selling and administrative expenses, the four finance lines, interest income, total and share-based depreciation, taxes paid, segment revenue and segment results, capital expenditure, investing and financing flows and the FX effect are not supplied; this limits full-year margin, cash-flow and coverage analysis, and the column carries only what the fourth-quarter 2025 release prints, including exploration expenses stated only to the nearest million. Severity: High. Action: supply the annual cash flow statement.

- Cash interest paid for the first quarters of 2025 and 2026 is not supplied because the first-quarter cash flow statements print no interest line; the six-month and second-quarter columns are equal, which implies none was paid in the first quarter, but the sources state no zero. - EBITDA (Reported) is not printed by Hudbay and is calculated here as results from operating activities plus cost-of-sales depreciation; for FY2025 and the last twelve months it includes the USD 322.3 million third-quarter 2025 impairment reversal and USD 14.9 million of consideration from a non-core project, so reported leverage and cover are flattered against the adjusted ratios. Severity: Medium. Action: read the adjusted ratios beside the reported ones.

- Several cells are not supplied because the source prints a dash: other (income) expenses for the second quarter of 2025, dividends paid in the second quarter of 2025, the revolver draw in the 2025 second-quarter and half-year columns, proceeds from the sale of the Copper World interest in the second quarter of 2026 and the 2025 second-quarter and half-year columns, the current portion of long-term debt at 30 June 2026 and the non-controlling interest at 31 December 2025; the printed totals show each is nil, but no zero is stated. Severity: Low. Action: none needed.

- Cash flow lines that a statement does not print are not supplied for that column, namely the revolver draw, the notes repurchase or repayment, and the proceeds from the Copper World sale in the columns that lack them; the printed lines add to the printed totals, so no material figure is missing. Severity: Low. Action: none needed.

- No covenant test, level, step-down, definition or headroom is printed for the revolving credit facilities; only statements of compliance at 30 June 2026, 31 March 2026 and 30 September 2025 appear, and the letter of credit facility is stated to have no financial covenants. Covenant headroom is therefore not established and none has been inferred. Severity: High. Action: supply the revolving credit agreements.

Severity: Low. Action: supply the municipal bond documents.

Severity: Medium. Action: supply the security documents.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Hudbay's business and governance profile supports creditors: a listed producer with no controlling shareholder identified in the sources, three operating regions and a record of debt reduction, but its Arizona growth programme now places the main risk in capital allocation.
Basis: 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-06-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, pages 5, 18; 6-K-EX-99.3_2025-12-31_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, page 5; calculation BG-01

Peru and Manitoba earn 85.1% of first-half 2026 revenue, so interruptions there matter more than the spread across three regions suggests. The Copper World partnership with Mitsubishi and the all-share Arizona Sonoran acquisition added growth without new group borrowing, though the venture holds USD 334.5 million of cash the group cannot use. The annual information form, the shareholder list and the venture agreement were not supplied, so control rights and restricted-payment capacity are not established.
Basis: 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-06-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, pages 8–9, 12, 30–32; 40-F_2025-12-31_form40f.htm.jsonl, pages 2–3; calculation BG-01
### Key findings

Ownership gives creditors alignment but little evidence to test it. The sources identify no sponsor or controlling shareholder and print no shareholder percentages, so a sponsor-extraction risk cannot be shown and cannot be ruled out from them. The one outside owner stated is Mitsubishi, which holds 30% of Copper World and has committed USD 600 million in two payments, and dividends paid in the first half of 2026 were only USD 5.7 million against operating cash flow of USD 508.3 million, or 1.1%.
Basis: 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-06-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, pages 3, 5, 9, 23; 40-F_2025-12-31_form40f.htm.jsonl, page 1; calculation BG-03

The operating base is diversified by metal and region but concentrated in two operations. Peru contributed 45.8% and Manitoba 39.2% of first-half 2026 revenue, with British Columbia at 14.9%, and copper and gold together were 90.6% of revenue from contracts, so a fall in either price or an interruption in Peru or Manitoba moves cash flow far more than the third region can offset. The company states that gold was 38% of second-quarter revenue.
Basis: 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-06-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, pages 10, 30–32; 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, page 17; calculation BG-01; calculation BG-02

Operating execution is the near-term swing factor and is currently mixed. In the second quarter port closures deferred concentrate shipments in Peru to July, a hoist gearbox failure and reduced workforce availability held back Manitoba, and Copper Mountain ran with its primary SAG mill constrained, with a cash cost of USD 3.22 per pound against an annual guidance range of USD 1.50 to USD 2.50. Adjusted EBITDA fell from USD 421.9 million in the first quarter to USD 321.2 million in the second, so execution rather than ownership is what moves creditor risk this year.
Basis: 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 2, 5, 10–14; calculation BG-05

Capital allocation has been creditor-friendly so far but is turning toward growth. Hudbay retired USD 102.5 million of the 2026 notes below par in 2025, repaid the remaining USD 472.5 million at maturity in April 2026, funded the Arizona Sonoran acquisition with new shares rather than debt and pays only a token dividend. Growth spending is now under way at Copper World, New Ingerbelle, Cactus and Mason, and British Columbia growth capital for 2026 was raised by about USD 30 million to USD 115 million.

Basis: 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-06-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, pages 8, 18; 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 4, 19–20; 6-K-EX-99.3_2025-12-31_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 5–6; calculation BG-04

Copper World is a controlled joint venture whose partner funding protects the parent but whose terms are not visible. Hudbay keeps 70% and consolidates it, Mitsubishi pays a further USD 180 million within 18 months and funds 30% of future equity calls, and Hudbay estimated its own share of remaining equity contributions at about USD 200 million with the first call no earlier than 2028. The joint venture board is chaired by the finance chief, which keeps control with Hudbay management, but the venture agreement was not supplied, so funding obligations, deadlock rights and distribution limits are not established.

Basis: 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-06-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, pages 5, 9; 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 15, 18; 6-K-EX-99.1_2025-09-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, pages 5, 13; calculation BG-05

Disclosure is strong on financial reporting and thin on creditor-specific terms. The auditor gave an unqualified opinion on internal control over financial reporting for 2025, no code-of-ethics waiver was granted, and no material off-balance-sheet arrangement exists, but the annual information form, covenant levels and the 2026 management discussion were not supplied and the interim statements are unaudited, so board composition, related-party dealings and restricted-payment capacity are not established.
Basis: 40-F_2025-12-31_form40f.htm.jsonl, pages 4–5; 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-06-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, pages 1, 19

Management turnover is orderly but concentrated in finance and operations. The finance chief becomes President and Chief Financial Officer, the chief operating officer retires at the end of September 2026 and is replaced from within, and new heads were named for the British Columbia and Arizona business units, which supports continuity but leaves one executive leading both capital markets and the Copper World venture board. No source confirms that the retirement took place by the 5 November 2026 cutoff.
Basis: 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 15–17

Permitting and community relations are an unpriced risk at Copper Mountain. The Lower Similkameen Indian Band applied for judicial review of the New Ingerbelle permit amendment on 23 March 2026, after permits were received on 19 February 2026, and the project is expected to give first production in late 2028; no amount, provision or funding obligation is stated, so the effect on creditors is directional only.
Basis: 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-03-31_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 14–15; 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 19–20
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against the supportive view is that capital allocation, not ownership, now carries the risk. Hudbay has two development projects in Arizona, an expansion in British Columbia and a Nevada project, the Copper World study is expected to show higher capital cost than the 2023 pre-feasibility study, and there is no sponsor to inject equity if a project overruns. The view would weaken if the venture agreement or credit agreements show that Hudbay must fund calls or allow payments out of the group, or if growth spending is funded by revolver draws, and it would strengthen if the sanction decision is paired with committed project financing and continued debt reduction.
Basis: 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 18–19, 22; 6-K-EX-99.1_2025-09-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, page 13; calculation BG-05

A second counterargument is that diversification is narrower than three regions imply, because Peru and Manitoba earn most of revenue and Manitoba depends on a workforce it is still building. A repeat of the 2025 wildfire shutdown, social unrest or a port closure in Peru would test that concentration, and the view would improve if Manitoba and British Columbia deliver the higher second-half production the company guides to.
Basis: 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 10–11; 6-K-EX-99.1_2025-09-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, page 3; calculation BG-01
### Limitations
- The annual information form and the shareholder list were not supplied, so the conclusion that no controlling shareholder exists rests on silence in the sources and is not a finding.
Basis: 40-F_2025-12-31_form40f.htm.jsonl, pages 2–3

- The Copper World venture agreement, the Wheaton stream agreements and the credit agreements were not supplied, so the conclusions on partner funding, distributions and restricted-payment capacity are directional and no legal capacity is assessed.
Basis: 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-06-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, pages 9, 19–20

- Management descriptions of operations, such as the share of gold in revenue and statements that production guidance is on track, are the company's own words and are used only as stated, so operating conclusions carry the weight of an issuer release, not an audit.
Basis: 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 2, 17

- Peru, Manitoba and British Columbia results are given for single quarters and a half year, so the conclusion that Peru and Manitoba dominate revenue does not test a full commodity cycle or a full year of 2025 segment results.
Basis: 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-06-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, pages 30–32

### Transaction summary and new debt issues

Copper World joint venture. Hudbay sold a 30% interest in Copper World to Mitsubishi in January 2026 under a subscription agreement dated 12 August 2025, for USD 600 million in total, of which USD 422.7 million of cash was received at closing and a further USD 180 million is due within 18 months. The transaction was accounted for as an equity transaction, so Hudbay keeps control and consolidates the project, and the cash received is reserved for the project and not available for general group use.
Basis: 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-06-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, page 9; 6-K-EX-99.1_2025-09-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, pages 5, 13; 6-K-EX-99.3_2025-12-31_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, page 5

Arizona Sonoran acquisition. Hudbay completed the acquisition of Arizona Sonoran on 24 June 2026 by issuing 46,794,082 shares valued at USD 1,135.6 million and cancelling shares it already held valued at USD 123.1 million, and accounted for it as an asset acquisition of the Cactus project. It brought USD 63.0 million of cash and USD 102.8 million of deferred land payments, and no new group borrowing was used.
Basis: 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-06-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, pages 8, 23; 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 18–19

Debt activity. Hudbay repaid the USD 472.5 million 2026 senior notes on 1 April 2026 using cash and a USD 272.0 million draw on its revolving credit facilities, leaving one series of senior notes due in April 2029 with USD 542.4 million of principal. On 24 June 2026 Copper World LLC issued USD 52.0 million of 4.50% solid waste disposal revenue bonds through the Arizona Industrial Development Authority, guaranteed by the parent and its primary operating subsidiaries, with an initial mandatory tender date of 2 July 2036 that the release describes as the due date, and the proceeds are held as restricted cash.
Basis: 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-06-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, pages 14, 18–20; 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-03-31_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, page 25; 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 4, 18

Other transactions. Hudbay acquired the remaining 25% of Copper Mountain on 30 April 2025 for total consideration of USD 35.9 million, of which USD 4.5 million was paid at closing, agreed amended terms with Wheaton on the Copper World stream in August 2025, with a USD 230 million initial deposit and up to USD 70 million more on a mill expansion, and amended an option agreement with JOGMEC and Marubeni on 22 January 2026 over a 10% interest in three Flin Flon projects.
Basis: 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-06-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, pages 9–10; 6-K-EX-99.1_2025-09-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, pages 5, 13; 6-K-EX-99.3_2025-12-31_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 25–26

# Fundamental credit for Hudbay Minerals Inc. (hbm), as of 2026-11-05
## Request

Fundamental credit for Hudbay Minerals Inc. (issuer id hbm), as of 2026-11-05, on the credit snapshot pathway. Scope: business, cost, cash-flow, liquidity, refinancing and governance synthesis from the seven supplied Hudbay filings and the earlier Source readiness, Financial foundation and Business & governance modules, with strengths, weaknesses, ranked drivers and monitoring triggers; no rating, covenant, recovery or position-sizing conclusion is drawn. Perimeter: consolidated Hudbay Minerals Inc., including the Copper World project entity (70% owned and consolidated) and Arizona Sonoran from 2026-06-24.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Hudbay's credit profile supports creditors today, with debt of USD 860.2 million at 0.68x adjusted EBITDA and no principal due before 2028, but earnings swing with metal prices and two operations, and growth spending is the main threat.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation FC-01; calculation FC-12

Quarterly adjusted EBITDA has ranged from USD 142.6 million to USD 421.9 million over 11 quarters, and gold credits pay for 85.1% of gross cash costs, so a gold price fall or a repeat of the 2025 wildfire and port interruptions would cut cash flow quickly. Cash taxes take 35.4% of adjusted EBITDA and the 2026 capital plan is USD 735.0 million, so free cash flow is modest against earnings. Covenant levels, the audited 2025 statements and the Copper World venture terms were not supplied, so the margin of safety against them is not established.

Basis: 6-K-EX-99.1_2025-09-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, page 47; 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 25–26; 6-K-EX-99.3_2025-12-31_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, page 34; calculation FC-03; calculation FC-05; calculation FC-09; calculation FC-10
### Key findings

Leverage is low and the maturity profile gives two years of runway, but 94.0% of principal falls due in two maturities five months apart. Total debt of USD 860.2 million is 0.68x trailing adjusted EBITDA and 0.56x reported EBITDA, down from 0.95x adjusted at the end of 2025 after the 2026 notes were repaid. Net debt excluding the USD 334.5 million of cash reserved for Copper World is USD 303.8 million, or 0.24x, and the pro forma effect of the dividend declared on 28 July 2026 on that net debt is not established. The USD 272.0 million revolver draw matures in November 2028, 24 months from the as-of date, and the USD 542.4 million of notes in April 2029, so both need refinancing in the same window, and nothing is due before it.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-06-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, pages 18–19; calculation FC-01; calculation FC-12; calculation FC-13

Earnings are volatile and concentrated in two operations, which is the risk a creditor underwrites, not leverage. Adjusted EBITDA has ranged by a factor of 2.96x between the weakest and strongest of 11 quarters, and Peru and Manitoba earned 85.1% of first-half 2026 revenue. In the third quarter of 2025 mandatory wildfire evacuations shut Manitoba for most of the quarter, a temporary mill suspension hit Peru and a USD 60 million concentrate shipment slipped into the next quarter, taking revenue down 35.3% and adjusted EBITDA to USD 142.6 million. In the second quarter of 2026 port closures again deferred a concentrate shipment to July, and a 19.5% fall in copper sold cut adjusted EBITDA 23.9%. Even so, debt would be 0.92x the trailing EBITDA at the end of the third quarter of 2025, the lowest of the last five quarter-ends, 1.05x the 2024 level and 1.51x if four quarters matched the weakest, so interruptions threaten liquidity timing before they threaten solvency.

Basis: 6-K-EX-99.1_2025-09-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, pages 3–4, 9, 47; 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 5, 7; 6-K-EX-99.3_2025-12-31_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, page 9; Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation FC-02; calculation FC-03; calculation FC-04; calculation FC-07; calculation FC-18

Gold by-product credits, not copper, are what make Hudbay a low-cost producer, which ties creditor risk to the gold price. In the second quarter of 2026 gold credits were 78.3% of all by-product credits and paid for 85.1% of the gross cash cost of USD 4.57 per pound, so the reported net cost of negative USD 0.40 per pound would be USD 3.50 without them; in the first quarter of 2026, with more gold sold, it was negative USD 1.80. Gross cash cost per pound rose 22.8% in a year on fuel and consumables, and the 2026 cost guidance assumes gold at USD 3,850 per ounce, so the cost position is a bet on gold holding at or above that level. Gold was 38% of 2025 revenue.
Basis: 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 2, 26; 6-K-EX-99.3_2025-12-31_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 4, 33; calculation FC-05; calculation FC-06; calculation FC-19

Production is stable at group level but its mix is moving away from the gold-rich Pampacancha ore, and guidance needs a stronger second half. Pampacancha was fully mined by December 2025, so Peru gold guidance is 76.5% below 2025 and Peru copper 3.1% below, while the group midpoint is 4.9% higher for copper and 8.7% lower for gold. First-half output is 45.3% of the copper midpoint and 46.2% of the gold midpoint, and the second-half plan depends on British Columbia reaching its target throughput once the primary grinding mill returns, on higher Manitoba grades and on the Peru pebble crushers. Management states that it has met copper guidance for 11 consecutive years, which supports the plan but does not test a second half this heavily loaded.
Basis: 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 2, 7, 11, 14; 6-K-EX-99.3_2025-12-31_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 2, 32–33; calculation FC-11; calculation FC-17

Cash conversion is moderate because taxes and capital absorb most of EBITDA. Taxes paid in the first half of 2026 were USD 262.8 million, 35.4% of adjusted EBITDA against 30.3% a year earlier, with tax expense at 43.1% of income before tax, so operating cash flow before working capital was 56.4% of adjusted EBITDA against 67.1%. Company-defined free cash flow of USD 413.0 million over the last 12 months is 32.5% of adjusted EBITDA, and the first-half working-capital inflow of USD 89.5 million is probably partly timing, because the concentrate deferred from the second quarter was delivered in July. Higher profits therefore bring higher tax outflows, and deleveraging capacity after growth spending is smaller than EBITDA suggests.
Basis: 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-06-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, pages 1–2; 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 5, 25; calculation FC-09

The 2026 capital plan is the main call on cash, and most near-term commitments can be cancelled. Planned spending of USD 735.0 million is 53.9% above 2025 actual spending, of which USD 135.0 million for Copper World is funded by the Mitsubishi proceeds, leaving group-funded capital of USD 600.0 million, 47.8% above 2025, before an increase of about USD 30 million for British Columbia growth capital. Sustaining capital costs of USD 167.1 million in the first half are 38.4% of the USD 435.0 million guided for the year on the closest comparable measure, which implies USD 267.9 million in the second half, and plans add about USD 30 million at Cactus and about USD 20 million at Mason in the second half. Of USD 202.6 million of capital commitments, USD 183.9 million can be terminated, which gives management a lever if cash weakens.

Basis: 6-K-EX-99.3_2025-12-31_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 6, 34; 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 4–5, 19, 22, 25, 28; 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-06-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, page 29; calculation FC-10; calculation FC-16

Copper World is funded for now but is an unresolved call on group cash. The venture holds USD 334.5 million reserved for it, Mitsubishi paid USD 420 million at closing in January 2026 and owes USD 180 million within 18 months, and Hudbay's own share of remaining equity contributions was estimated at about USD 200 million, with no call before 2028. That estimate is about 48.4% of trailing free cash flow, but it was made in 2025 from the 2023 pre-feasibility study, while the feasibility study is now expected to show higher capital cost, was expected in mid-2026 and was still in progress at the latest document, and the second-quarter release still lists consummating the definitive Wheaton agreement for the enhanced stream as an assumption. The sanction decision is expected after the date of the latest document, so its outcome is not established.

### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against the supportive view is that leverage is measured on trailing adjusted EBITDA that the company calls a record, struck at high metal prices, while the cost advantage and the profit after tax both depend on gold. If gold fell below the USD 3,850 per ounce assumed in 2026 guidance while a Peru or Manitoba interruption recurred, quarterly EBITDA could return towards the USD 142.6 million seen in 2025 just as USD 600.0 million of group-funded capital, Copper World and the 2028 and 2029 maturities converge. The view would weaken if the sanction decision commits group cash beyond the USD 200 million estimate, if the revolver is drawn again to fund growth, or if covenant levels prove tight on a definition the company does not print. It would strengthen if the USD 272.0 million draw were repaid from cash flow, if the 2028 and 2029 maturities were refinanced early, and if covenant levels showed wide headroom.

Basis: 6-K-EX-99.1_2025-09-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, page 9; 6-K-EX-99.3_2025-12-31_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 33–34; 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 18, 26; calculation FC-02; calculation FC-10; calculation FC-16

The best argument for a stronger view is the track record and the size of the cushion: management states that it has met copper guidance for 11 consecutive years, the trailing year to the weakest recent quarter-end still leaves debt at 0.92x, 90.8% of near-term capital commitments can be cancelled, and the group repaid USD 472.5 million of notes at maturity without new equity. That argument is sound for the next 12 months to 24 months and is the reason the view is supportive, but it says little about 2028 and 2029, when growth capital, the Copper World funding calls and both maturities coincide and the sources give no covenant, rating or market-price evidence to test refinancing access.

### Business model, ownership and revenue durability

Revenue is durable in volume but not in price: Hudbay sells copper, gold, silver, zinc and molybdenum priced off market quotations, and receivables on provisionally priced concentrate are marked to forward prices each quarter, so revenue moves with metal markets rather than contracts. Copper and gold together were 90.6% of revenue from contracts in the first half, Peru and Manitoba earned 85.1% of revenue, and 38% of 2025 revenue was gold. The sources do not name customers, state offtake terms or show a customer concentration, so buyer concentration is not established. The consequence for creditors is high operating leverage to prices with low contractual visibility, offset by 90.8% terminable commitments and low leverage.

Ownership supports creditor alignment but cannot be tested: Hudbay is listed, no controlling shareholder or sponsor is identified, Mitsubishi owns 30% of the Copper World joint venture, and former Arizona Sonoran shareholders received new shares in June 2026 instead of cash. A listed issuer with no sponsor has less extraction risk, and also has no outside equity support if a project overruns. Subsidiary guarantees and structural subordination to the secured revolver are not visible in the sources.

### Cost structure and margin resilience

Margins can be defended against moderate volume shortfalls, since adjusted EBITDA margin was 50.9% in the second quarter of 2026 against 55.7% in the first after revenue fell 16.6%, and they are exposed to input inflation and to gold. Onsite cost per pound rose 25.9% in a year to USD 4.23, on higher fuel and consumable prices and, in British Columbia, equipment maintenance timing, and the second quarter showed operating deleverage as adjusted EBITDA fell 23.9% on a 19.5% fall in copper sold. Three features cushion the margin: employee profit sharing, which reached USD 36.1 million in the fourth quarter of 2025 at high margins and was lower in Peru in the second quarter of 2026; a new Peru power contract and lower treatment and refining charges; and a record British Columbia mining rate. Adjusted EBITDA margin has ranged from 41.1% to 55.7% across the periods supplied.

### Market forces and policy

Five forces matter to credit mainly through price-taking, entry barriers and input costs. Rivalry and substitutes act through metal prices, which Hudbay does not set, and its hedges are small. New entrants face long permitting, as the New Ingerbelle permit and the judicial review application against it show, which protects the existing production base but delays Hudbay's own growth. Buyer power cannot be assessed because customers are not named, and substitutes are not discussed in the sources. Supplier power shows in fuel and consumable inflation, Manitoba labour shortages that required a mining contractor, and equipment failures such as a hoist gearbox, each of which raised unit costs in the second quarter of 2026.

Political and regulatory factors are material for Peru and for permits. The company lists the Peruvian political and social environment as an assumption behind guidance, 2025 mine plan changes were made during social unrest, community agreement payments rose to USD 13.0 million in the second quarter from USD 3.7 million in the first, and the New Ingerbelle permit faces a judicial review application from the Lower Similkameen Indian Band. Costs in Canadian dollars against US dollar prices are a further exposure, because guidance assumes a fixed exchange rate and no sensitivity is printed.

### Outlook

The outlook for the next 12 months to 24 months is supportive but back-end loaded. Tailwinds are the delivery of concentrate deferred into July, the second-half ramp-up in British Columbia, higher Manitoba output, the Peru pebble crushers, copper hedges struck above the copper price assumed in guidance, improved consolidated cost guidance of negative USD 0.45 to negative USD 0.25 per pound, and the higher Constancia mill permit. Headwinds are fuel and consumable costs, dependence on a repaired primary grinding mill in British Columbia, Manitoba labour, cash taxes and the higher capital plan. These support liquidity and margins in the near term and leave the second-half guidance exposed to execution.

Basis: 6-K-EX-99.3_2026-06-30_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, pages 2, 5, 11, 14, 20; 6-K-EX-99.1_2026-06-30_exhibit99-1.htm.jsonl, page 28; 6-K-EX-99.3_2025-12-31_exhibit99-3.htm.jsonl, page 33; calculation FC-11; calculation FC-15; calculation FC-19

The outlook for three to five years turns on timing. The Copper World sanction, the Arizona Sonoran development, New Ingerbelle first production in late 2028 and full 1901 production in late 2027 add copper and gold volume, while Peru grades re-sequence towards higher production in 2027 and 2028. The same years carry the November 2028 revolver and April 2029 note maturities and the first Copper World equity call, so deleveraging can continue only if growth is paced and the refinancing is completed before the facilities become current in late 2027 and early 2028.

### Downside scenario

The realistic downside is a repeat of the 2025 sequence while gold weakens and Copper World spending begins. The initiating condition is a fall in gold below the USD 3,850 per ounce used for 2026 guidance together with an interruption in Peru or Manitoba, both of which occurred within 12 months. The first operational break is deferred shipments or a mine shutdown, as in the third quarter of 2025, when revenue fell 35.3% and adjusted EBITDA fell to USD 142.6 million. Lower gold credits then raise net cash cost directly, since every dollar of gold credit lost falls straight to EBITDA, while the cash tax charge falls only with profit. Free cash flow turns negative for a quarter, as it did in the third quarter of 2025, and the revolver, with USD 153.7 million undrawn, absorbs the gap. Leverage would be 0.92x on the trailing EBITDA at the weakest recent quarter-end, 1.05x on the 2024 level and 1.51x on four weak quarters. Management can cancel USD 183.9 million of commitments, defer Cactus and Mason spending and keep dividends at their small level, so resilience looks sufficient to avoid liquidity distress through 2027 on the stated figures. The observable triggers are quarterly EBITDA below USD 142.6 million, further revolver draws, a Copper World sanction without committed non-group funding, and no refinancing plan by late 2027.

### Overall credit view

Overall, Hudbay presents an adequate business profile supported by low leverage, a gold-driven cost position and cancellable capital commitments, but credit quality is constrained by concentration in two operations, exposure to gold and copper prices and a growth programme that peaks as its debt matures. Cash-flow durability appears adequate because company-defined free cash flow of USD 413.0 million over the last 12 months has absorbed taxes and sustaining capital, but conversion falls as profits rise. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on metal prices in 2027, the Copper World outcome and covenant headroom that the sources do not show. The primary downside path is a gold price fall or a Peru or Manitoba interruption coinciding with Copper World funding and the 2028 and 2029 maturities. Further analysis would require covenant levels, the audited 2025 statements, the Copper World venture and Wheaton agreements, customer terms and market evidence on pricing and ratings.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation FC-01; calculation FC-09; calculation FC-12
Fundamental credit is complete. Top risk: earnings concentration and gold dependence meeting the Copper World funding decision and the 2028 and 2029 maturities.
### Strengths and weaknesses

Strengths, in order of weight. First, low leverage with no principal due before 2028: debt of USD 860.2 million is 0.68x adjusted EBITDA, so a weak year would not by itself threaten debt service. Second, a gold-driven cost position: credits paid for 85.1% of gross cash cost, which kept adjusted EBITDA at 50.9% to 55.7% of revenue in 2026, though it depends on gold. Third, liquidity and flexibility: USD 710.1 million of liquidity excluding Copper World cash and 90.8% of capital commitments that can be cancelled give management levers in a downturn. Fourth, creditor-aligned financial policy: debt fell USD 148.4 million in the first half, the dividend is 1.1% of operating cash flow and no sponsor is identified, which lowers the risk of cash extraction.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation FC-01; calculation FC-05; calculation FC-08; calculation FC-13; calculation FC-16; calculation FC-17

Weaknesses, in order of weight. First, concentration and interruption record: 85.1% of revenue comes from Peru and Manitoba and adjusted EBITDA has ranged by a factor of 2.96x between quarters, so cash flow can fall fast. Second, a maturity cluster: 94.0% of principal falls due in November 2028 and April 2029 and 60.4% of the revolver is drawn, so the refinancing is a single event and availability is already thinner. Third, a growing capital programme: USD 735.0 million planned in 2026, 53.9% above 2025, plus Copper World funding of about USD 200 million from 2028 and a higher-cost feasibility study. Fourth, cash leakage: taxes paid were 35.4% of first-half adjusted EBITDA. Fifth, opacity: no covenant levels, guarantor structure or ranking of USD 324.5 million of other claims.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation FC-02; calculation FC-03; calculation FC-04; calculation FC-09; calculation FC-10; calculation FC-12; calculation FC-14; calculation FC-16

The nine-dimension profile is as follows. Scale and market position is average: revenue was USD 2,211.0 million in 2025 across three regions, but Hudbay sets no prices. Competitive advantage is average: the cost position rests on by-product credits, not on a structural moat. Business diversification is average: five metals and three regions, but 85.1% of revenue from two operations. Cost and capex flexibility is average: 90.8% of commitments can be terminated, but gross cost per pound rose 22.8%. Margin stability is average: adjusted EBITDA margin ranged from 41.1% to 55.7%. Free cash flow stability is average: the quarter-to-quarter swing is wide and conversion is 32.5% of EBITDA. Ability to refinance is average: a USD 52.0 million municipal bond was placed in June 2026 at 4.5%, but no rating or market quote was supplied. Liquidity is strong on the company's definition: USD 1,044.6 million, or 0.83x total debt after removing reserved cash, and no maturity before 2028. Financial policy and governance is average: creditor-friendly behaviour with unseen covenants and restricted-payment limits. The trend is improving leverage and thinner revolver availability, and the key missing data are covenants, audited 2025 statements, customer terms and market evidence.
